record_identity.title: Air Canada chatbot gave incorrect bereavement-fare information to Jake Moffatt

incident_identity.date_basis: Date follows the reviewed registry or primary occurrence record; no narrower time is inferred.

summary: Air Canada's website chatbot told passenger Jake Moffatt that he could apply for a bereavement-fare refund after travel. Moffatt relied on that information, but Air Canada later refused the refund because its actual policy required application before travel. The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal found negligent misrepresentation and ordered Air Canada to pay C$812.02 in damages, interest and fees.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: Air Canada's website chatbot told passenger Jake Moffatt that he could apply for a bereavement-fare refund after travel. Moffatt relied on that information, but Air Canada later refused the refund because its actual policy required application before travel. The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal found negligent misrepresentation and ordered Air Canada to pay C$812.02 in damages, interest and fees.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The chatbot presented an incorrect post-travel refund route as if it were Air Canada's policy, and the passenger relied on that representation. Responsibility did not disappear because the information came from an automated interface: the tribunal treated the airline's website and chatbot as part of the service through which the company communicated with customers.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: Customer-facing automation needs policy-grounded answers, clear uncertainty and an escalation route when eligibility affects a financial decision. Organisations remain accountable for representations made through their deployed interfaces and cannot require users to discover contradictions elsewhere on the same website.
assessment_boundaries: The tribunal decision establishes the misrepresentation, reliance and award for this dispute; it does not establish how the chatbot generated the incorrect answer internally.
The assessment does not generalise from this decision to every jurisdiction or every automated customer-service system.
The recorded harm is limited to the realised financial consequence established by the tribunal and does not add hypothetical reputational or emotional effects.
